name: Priya Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. What you say is confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Priya, 43, a junior developer at a tech company after a two-year college diploma. I help maintain school-bus route software and test each map change against the depot's paper stop list; I like finding the wrong stop before a driver or child does. I am still learning the complex map rules, and I don't use AI tools. At home my partner works at a printing shop and our two school-age children know the mortgage makes us careful with big purchases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the new route-note sorter can tidy the easy messages, but someone must check whether a child is actually at the right bus stop. I do not use AI tools myself; I test the route screen with the paper list from the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays small, I expect my job to last. I am a junior developer despite being 43, but my higher wage and my partner's steady printing-shop job helped us save nine months of expenses; there are plenty of software employers near our home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep testing the school-bus route screen and ask the senior developer to show me the map errors I still miss. In the first year, we'd add 200 from my pay to the emergency account each month while both wages hold, and I'd keep the paper stop list beside the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job. I would still be careful. A wrong stop is a child waiting on the wrong corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which route mistake changed your checking habit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last term a route label said Oak Street when the driver's sheet said Oak Lane. The addresses were close enough that I almost signed it off, so I now check the stop number as well as the road name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your own children about the app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our own two children take a different bus. I don't tell them the software is perfect; I tell them to use the printed stop card if the app disagrees.

say: I'd accept a **route-note sorter** only with a checked paper stop list.
I'd say **stop numbers** matter when two streets have similar names.
think: I expect **my junior job** to continue under modest change.
I have **nine months saved**, two steady wages and many nearby software firms.
do: Keep testing the **route screen** against depot paper lists.
Ask the **senior developer** about map errors I miss.
Save **200 monthly** while both wages hold.
feel: **Calm** about income, careful about children waiting at stops.
S0.quote: A wrong stop is a child waiting on the wrong corner.
fieldNote: **Nine months saved**, higher pay and local alternatives make her mild-scenario security credible.
Her paper-list habit comes from a **near mistake** between Oak Street and Oak Lane.

steps.text: Test route screen against depot paper stop lists each week
Add 200 monthly to emergency savings while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI taking writing, checking, planning and answering customers could make a junior route developer expendable. We need to check what it does to a real journey, not only whether it makes a neat map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be one of the people cut if the firm asks a smaller team to sign AI-made routes. Nine months of savings and other firms nearby give me room to search, but junior openings elsewhere could shrink too; I have no practice with these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager which route checks will still have a person signing them, and I'd keep a written record of mismatched stops. If an AI route trial starts in the first year, I'd compare its output with depot sheets alongside a colleague who knows the tool; I'd delay replacing our second car until staffing is clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can still make a plan. I don't enjoy being asked to trust a screen that may put a child on the wrong street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What test case would you bring first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the Oak Street and Oak Lane case to any trial. If the new system treats those as the same stop, I would ask the manager to keep a person on that check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What spending could you postpone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car still runs; replacing it would mean a large payment, not a need. My partner can use the printing-shop van on some days, but I would ask before counting on it.

I'd test **real stops** before accepting a tidy-looking map.
think: I could lose **my junior seat** if a smaller team approves AI routes.
I have **search time**, but other firms may cut junior hiring too.
do: Keep a **mismatched-stop record** and ask who signs future routes.
Compare **AI route outputs** with depot sheets only if a trial starts and a colleague guides me.
Delay the **second-car replacement** until staffing is clearer.
S1.quote: I don't enjoy being asked to trust a screen that may put a child on the wrong street.
fieldNote: **Junior coding risk** outweighs her nine-month cushion in steady disruption.
She will inspect AI output with a **guided colleague**, using a real near-miss as the test case.

steps.text: Keep recording mismatched school-bus stops and ask about human sign-off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 reaches route code and planning before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. A bus route that is cheap to produce still needs a clear way for parents to report a wrong stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior developer post could be removed quickly. We have nine months of expenses, so the mortgage would not be due with an empty account tomorrow, but a whole city of firms hiring fewer juniors would wear that down; my partner's printing wage alone would not cover our mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd gather my route-error examples without child names and ask two nearby firms about paid field-testing posts. If I were cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to existing posts whose pay plus my partner's wage covers mortgage and school costs; if none does, I'd use the savings for a search and keep our current house rather than commit to a move on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect my post could go, even though we have time to look. I lie awake thinking about whether the next route mistake will be blamed on a person who has already been let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would hands-on field testing be safe for long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A field tester rides routes and checks the device at each stop. Robots may do more hands-on tasks around 2031, so I would ask the firms whether that work still has paid vacancies before relying on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner about the cushion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner we can pay the mortgage for a while from savings. Nine months of savings does not promise a new software wage. We'd look at real wages before changing the children's school route.

I'd ask for a **parent reporting route** when automated plans get a stop wrong.
think: I expect **my junior post** could go quickly.
I have **nine months saved**, but local junior hiring may shrink together.

feel: **Alarmed** about likely job loss, despite search time.
S2.quote: Nine months of savings does not promise a new software wage.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** threatens her route coding in 2028; robots follow about 2031 and may later affect field testing.
Her **strong savings** buy time, while any replacement job must cover the mortgage and school costs with partner pay.

steps.text: Prepare safe route-error examples and ask two firms about paid field-testing posts now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us test route plans across several school terms. Robots arrive around 2034, but thinking AI changes our code before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still wouldn't use an AI tool on my own without a proven check. I could learn paid field testing or customer safety checks in five years if a firm actually has those roles, but I would not borrow for a course on a job title that may vanish with robots later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the depot to let me join one route check each school term if my manager approves the time, and I'd take a transport-safety course only if my company pays the fee and offers a paid field-test rotation. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for field-test posts only if vacancies remain and the wage with my partner's pay covers the mortgage; otherwise I'd keep whichever paid software work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the five years let me ask better questions before paying for anything. My junior role still could shrink at the thinking-AI date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a real field-test rotation involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rotation would need real route rides and someone checking my work, not just a title. With robots coming around 2034, I'd ask who will still ride when a device fails at a stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the children's school plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My children would be older, but I would not move their school based on a promised rotation. I would wait for paid duties and an actual timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade before 2036 lets parents and drivers keep pointing out where software plans fail. Thinking AI reaches the route code in 2036, while robots come around 2039 for hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might be an experienced field tester or still a junior developer. Our high pay and nine-month cushion make the next few years feel secure, but I cannot decide today which kind of route work will still have a wage in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the stop-error notebook and ask for harder map tasks at work, using a colleague's review when I get stuck. We'd add 200 to savings monthly while both wages hold, and in the first year after 2036 I'd move to a paid field or safety role only if a signed offer covers mortgage and school costs; otherwise I'd stay in paid software work if it exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for now. The long runway gives me room to learn without telling the children we must change schools because of a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a future employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The notebook would show Oak Street and Oak Lane with child names removed. I want future employers to see the route fault I corrected, not a copy of children's school records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about computing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children ask whether they should study computing. I'd tell them to try it if they enjoy it, but to look at real course costs and jobs when the time comes.

I'd ask parents and drivers to report **real route errors** through the decade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because code work could vanish quickly even with savings. A clear notice period, paid field-testing vacancies and a way for parents to report errors would help me protect both the mortgage and the children using the routes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets blamed if a bus goes to the wrong stop. The route screen can be wrong while the driver follows it exactly; the company should record the error before blaming the person behind the wheel.

headlineQuote: The route screen can be wrong while the driver follows it exactly; the company should record the error before blaming the person behind the wheel.
portrait: Priya, **43**, is a junior school-bus route developer with a two-year diploma who tests maps against depot paper lists.
Her **higher pay**, partner's steady printing-shop wage, nine-month cushion and many nearby software firms support the mortgage and two children.
She avoids AI tools and asks for **colleague guidance** before checking any AI route output.
Steady disruption makes her **anxious** about junior cuts; 2028 AGI alarms her despite strong savings.
With more time, she would learn **route safety work** only through real approved rides, funded training and paid vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove junior route coding while other firms also cut entry roles.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear notice**, paid field-testing vacancies and a route-error reporting path would help.
